sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Browser error monitoring setup
sections.what: Starts Sentry in the browser with the project address, sampling rates, and session replay. Replays record text and media as hidden, and every error session is recorded.
sections.why: Lets the team find and understand problems that users hit in production without asking them to report bugs.
sections.watch_out: Turning off the masking options would expose private health text in replay recordings.

summary: Starts the Sentry error and performance monitoring tool in the user's browser and turns on session replay with text and media hidden.
purpose: Records errors and slow pages from real users in the browser so developers can see problems in production. Replay lets developers watch what happened before an error, with private content hidden.
why: The comments say this is the standard Sentry setup for Next.js. The privacy settings hide text and media, which fits a health app, though the reason is not stated in the code.
how: The file reads the Sentry address from an environment variable, sets how many page loads are measured, turns on replays for all sessions with errors and for ten percent of other sessions, and masks text and media in those replays. It also exports the router hook Next.js calls on page changes.
inputs: The public Sentry address from the NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN environment variable, plus the built in browser events.
outputs: Error reports, performance traces, and replay recordings sent to Sentry.
risks: If the Sentry address variable is missing, monitoring silently does nothing. Sampling rates set here control how much data is sent and how much it costs. Replay masking must stay on for a health app.
debug: If errors do not appear in Sentry, check that NEXT_PUBLIC_SENTRY_DSN is set in the deployment. Check that the rates are not zero. If replays show private text, confirm that the masking options are still set.
